{{Short description|Module over the non-commutative Dieudonné ring}}
In mathematics, a '''Dieudonné module''' introduced by {{harvs|txt|last=Dieudonné|first=Jean|authorlink=Jean Dieudonné|year1=1954|year2=1957b}},  is a [[module (mathematics)|module]] over the non-commutative '''Dieudonné ring''', which is generated over the ring of [[Witt vector]]s by two special  endomorphisms <math>F</math> and <math>V</math> called the [[Frobenius endomorphism|Frobenius]] and [[Verschiebung operator|Verschiebung]] operators. They are used for studying finite flat commutative group schemes.

Finite flat commutative group schemes over a perfect [[field (mathematics)|field]] <math>k</math> of positive characteristic <math>p</math> can be studied by transferring their geometric structure to a (semi-)linear-algebraic setting. The basic object is the Dieudonné ring 

:<math>D=W(k)\{F,V\}/(FV-p)</math>, 

which is a quotient of the ring of noncommutative polynomials, with coefficients in [[Witt vectors]] of <math>k</math>.  The endomorphisms <math>F</math> and <math>V</math> are the Frobenius and Verschiebung operators, and they may act nontrivially on the Witt vectors. Dieudonné and [[Pierre Cartier (mathematician)|Pierre Cartier]] constructed an [[antiequivalence of categories]] between finite commutative group schemes over <math>k</math> of order a power of <math>p</math> and modules over <math>D</math> with finite <math>W(k)</math>-length. The Dieudonné module functor in one direction is given by homomorphisms into the [[Sheaf of modules|abelian sheaf]] <math>CW</math> of Witt co-vectors. This sheaf is more or less dual to the sheaf of Witt vectors (which is in fact representable by a [[group scheme]]), since it is constructed by taking a [[direct limit]] of finite length Witt vectors under successive Verschiebung maps <math>V\colon W_n \to W_{n+1}</math>, and then completing. Many properties of commutative group schemes can be seen by examining the corresponding Dieudonné modules, e.g., connected <math>p</math>-group schemes correspond to <math>D</math>-modules for which <math>F</math> is nilpotent, and étale group schemes correspond to modules for which <math>F</math> is an isomorphism.

Dieudonné theory exists in a somewhat more general setting than finite flat groups over a field. [[Tadao Oda]]'s 1967 thesis gave a connection between Dieudonné modules and the first [[de Rham cohomology]] of [[Abelian variety|abelian varieties]], and at about the same time, [[Alexander Grothendieck]] suggested that there should be a crystalline version of the theory that could be used to analyze <math>p</math>-divisible groups. Galois actions on the group schemes transfer through the equivalences of categories, and the associated deformation theory of Galois representations was used in [[Andrew Wiles]]'s work on the [[Shimura–Taniyama conjecture]].

==Dieudonné rings==
If <math>k</math> is a perfect field of characteristic <math>p</math>, its ring of [[Witt vector]]s consists of sequences <math>(w_1,w_2,w_3,\dots)</math> of elements of <math>k</math>, and has an endomorphism <math>\sigma</math> induced by the [[Frobenius endomorphism]] of <math>k</math>, so <math>(w_1,w_2,w_3,\dots)^\sigma=(w^p_1,w^p_2,w^p_3,\dots)</math>. The '''Dieudonné ring''', often denoted by <math>E_k</math> or <math>D_k</math>, is the non-commutative ring over <math>W(k)</math> generated by 2 elements <math>F</math> and <math>V</math> subject to the relations
:<math>FV = VF = p</math>
:<math>Fw = w^\sigma F</math>
:<math>wV = Vw^\sigma</math>.

It is a <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>-graded ring, where the piece of  degree <math>{n\in\mathbb{Z}}</math> is a 1-dimensional [[free module]] over <math>W(k)</math>, spanned by <math>V^{-n}</math> if <math>n\leq 0</math> and by <math>F^n</math> if <math>n\geq 0</math>.
 
Some authors define the Dieudonné ring to be the completion of the ring above for the ideal generated by <math>F</math> and <math>V</math>.

==Dieudonné modules and groups==

Special sorts of modules over the Dieudonné ring correspond to certain algebraic group schemes. For example, finite length modules over the Dieudonné ring form an [[abelian category]] equivalent to the opposite of the category of finite commutative <math>p</math>-group schemes over <math>k</math>.

==Examples==

* If <math>X</math> is the constant group scheme <math>\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}</math> over <math>k</math>, then its corresponding Dieudonné module <math> \mathbf{D}(X) </math> is <math>k</math> with <math> F = \mathrm{Frob}_k</math> and <math> V = 0 </math>.
* For the scheme of <math>p</math>-th roots of unity <math>X = \mu_p</math>, then its corresponding Dieudonné module is <math> \mathbf{D}(X) = k</math> with <math> F = 0 </math> and <math> V = \mathrm{Frob}_k^{-1}</math>.
* For <math> X = \alpha_p</math>, defined as the kernel of the Frobenius <math> \mathbb{G}_{a} \to \mathbb{G}_{a}</math>, the Dieudonné module is <math> \mathbf{D}(X) = k</math> with <math> F = V = 0 </math>.
* If <math> X = E[p] </math> is the <math>p</math>-torsion of an elliptic curve over <math>k</math> (with <math>p</math>-torsion in <math>k</math>), then the Dieudonné module depends on whether <math>E</math> is [[supersingular elliptic curve|supersingular]] or not.

==Dieudonné–Manin classification theorem==

The Dieudonné–Manin classification theorem was proved by {{harvs|txt|last=Dieudonné | author-link=Jean Dieudonné|year=1955}} and {{harvs|txt|first=Yuri|last=Manin|authorlink=Yuri Manin| year=1963}}. It describes the structure of Dieudonné modules over an algebraically closed field <math>k</math> up to "isogeny". More precisely, it classifies the finitely generated modules over <math>D_k[1/p]</math>, where <math>D_k</math> is the Dieudonné ring. The category of such modules is semisimple, so every module is a direct sum of simple modules. The simple modules are the modules <math>E_{s/r}</math> where <math>r</math> and <math>s</math> are coprime integers with <math>r>0</math>.  The module <math>E_{s/r}</math> has a basis over <math>W(k)[1/p]</math> of the form <math>v, Fv, F^2 v,\dots, F^{r-1}v</math> for some element <math>v</math>, and <math>F^r v=p^s v</math>. The rational number <math>s/r</math> is called the slope of the module.

==The Dieudonné module of a group scheme==

If <math>G</math> is a commutative group scheme, its Dieudonné module <math>D(G)</math> is defined to be <math>\text{Hom}(G,W)</math>, defined as <math>\lim_n\text{Hom}(G,W_n)</math> where <math>W</math> is the formal Witt group scheme and 
<math>W_n</math> is the truncated Witt group scheme of Witt vectors of length <math>n</math>. 

The Dieudonné module gives antiequivalences between various sorts of commutative group schemes and left modules over the Dieudonné ring <math>D</math>.
*Finite commutative group schemes of <math>p</math>-power order correspond to <math>D</math> modules that have finite length over <math>W</math>.
*Unipotent affine commutative group schemes correspond to <math>D</math> modules that are <math>V</math>-torsion.
*<math>p</math>-divisible groups correspond to <math>D</math>-modules that are finitely generated free <math>W</math>-modules, at least over perfect fields. 

==Dieudonné crystal==

A Dieudonné crystal is a [[crystal (mathematics)|crystal]] <math>D</math> together with homomorphisms <math>F:D^p\to D</math>  and <math>V:D\to D^p</math> satisfying the relations <math>VF=p</math> (on <math>D^p</math>), <math>FV=p</math> (on <math>D</math>). Dieudonné crystals were introduced by {{harvtxt|Grothendieck|1966}} and were developed in depth by Berthelot, Breen and Messing using [[crystalline cohomology]]. They play the same role for classifying algebraic groups over schemes that Dieudonné modules play for classifying algebraic groups over fields. Very recently, the notion of [[prismatic cohomology]] (due to Bhatt and Scholze) has been used by Anschütz-Le Bras, Madapusi-Mondal, and Mondal to obtain generalisations of the notion of Dieudonné crystal in mixed characteristic.
